[2024 fall ms applied — problem 4]

Multiple regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, X_3$, $n = 25$, SS(Total) $= 248.0$; table of SSReg for all predictor subsets (SSReg($X_1,X_2,X_3) = 181.8$, SSReg($X_1,X_2) = 145.2$, etc.), $\alpha = 0.05$. (1) Global F-test of $H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0$. (2) Compute the extra SSReg$(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)$. (3) Test whether $X_3$ can be dropped. (4) Write the first row of the reduced-model $X$-matrix testing $H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_3 = 0$ (first obs: $Y=10, X_1=1985, X_2=59.7, X_3=2205$).

response.text:
Let the full model be

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\beta_2X_{i2}+\beta_3X_{i3}+\varepsilon_i,
\]

with \(n=25\). The full-model regression sum of squares is

\[
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)=181.8,
\]

and

\[
SST=248.0.
\]

Thus the full-model error sum of squares is

\[
SSE_{\text{full}}=SST-SSReg_{\text{full}}
=248.0-181.8=66.2.
\]

The full model has \(3\) predictors plus an intercept, so

\[
df_E=n-4=25-4=21.
\]

Hence

\[
MSE_{\text{full}}=\frac{66.2}{21}=3.1524.
\]

---

## (1) Global \(F\)-test of \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)

The hypotheses are

\[
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0
\]

versus

\[
H_a:\text{at least one of } \beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3 \neq 0.
\]

The regression degrees of freedom are \(3\), so

\[
MSReg=\frac{181.8}{3}=60.6.
\]

The global \(F\)-statistic is

\[
F=\frac{MSReg}{MSE}
=\frac{60.6}{3.1524}
=19.22.
\]

At \(\alpha=0.05\),

\[
F_{0.95;3,21}\approx 3.07.
\]

Since

\[
19.22>3.07,
\]

we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence that at least one of the predictors is linearly associated with \(Y\).

---

## (2) Compute \(SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)\)

The extra regression sum of squares for adding \(X_3\) after \(X_1,X_2\) is

\[
SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)
=
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)-SSReg(X_1,X_2).
\]

Given

\[
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)=181.8,
\qquad
SSReg(X_1,X_2)=145.2,
\]

we get

\[
SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)=181.8-145.2=36.6.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)=36.6.}
\]

---

## (3) Test whether \(X_3\) can be dropped

We test

\[
H_0:\beta_3=0
\]

given that \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) remain in the model, versus

\[
H_a:\beta_3\neq 0.
\]

The extra sum of squares for \(X_3\) given \(X_1,X_2\) is \(36.6\), with numerator degrees of freedom \(1\). Thus

\[
F
=
\frac{SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)/1}{MSE_{\text{full}}}
=
\frac{36.6}{3.1524}
=11.61.
\]

At \(\alpha=0.05\),

\[
F_{0.95;1,21}\approx 4.32.
\]

Since

\[
11.61>4.32,
\]

we reject \(H_0:\beta_3=0\). Therefore, \(X_3\) contributes significantly after adjusting for \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), so \(X_3\) should not be dropped.

---

## (4) First row of the reduced-model \(X\)-matrix testing \(H_0:\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)

Testing

\[
H_0:\beta_2=\beta_3=0
\]

means the reduced model keeps only the intercept and \(X_1\):

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\varepsilon_i.
\]

Thus the reduced-model design matrix has columns

\[
1,\quad X_1.
\]

For the first observation,

\[
Y=10,\qquad X_1=1985,\qquad X_2=59.7,\qquad X_3=2205.
\]

Only the intercept and \(X_1\) appear in the reduced \(X\)-matrix, so the first row is

\[
\boxed{(1,\ 1985)}.
\]

The value \(Y=10\) is part of the response vector, not the design matrix.
